summary: One capability, `src/modules/assistant-replies/`, owns assistant reply generation for both the browser SSE stream and the background job. A `POST` Route Handler at `src/app/api/assistant/replies/stream/route.ts` owns HTTP, commit state, a channel-owned AbortController, the sliding idle timeout, in-band post-commit failures, and the single unexpected-failure report; a queue-callback Route Handler drives `job.ts` with its own deadline, retry, idempotency, and dead-letter decisions. Both channels share one silent application operation (`application/generate-reply.ts`) and one capability-shaped generator port, with liveness passed in as a named policy input so the job never inherits stream idle-timeout semantics. The stakeholder's reuse of the shared operation and port is adopted; the proposed Server Action plus ordinary request retry is not, because an action cannot own commit state, a sliding idle timer, or an in-band post-commit error, and replaying a committed stream duplicates delivered tokens — resume by event id instead.

tree.purpose: POST SSE boundary: route-local input decode, authentication, channel-owned AbortController, pre-commit status mapping, response headers/commit, sole unexpected-failure report.
Queue callback boundary: signature verification, durable idempotency, calls job.ts, maps outcome to complete/retry/dead-letter, reports once.
Public streaming contract (openReplyStream) consumed only by the stream route; publishes the event union and acquisition-before-commit guarantee.
Public worker contract (runReplyGeneration) consumed only by the job callback route; takes deadline and attempt, returns a typed job outcome.
Browser-safe surface: the stream event contract, its decoder, and the useReplyStream hook for app/** client components.
Pure prompt invariants: non-empty, max length, allowed model tier. No framework or provider imports.
Provider-neutral event union (chunk/error/done) and event-id cursor rules, shared by stream.ts and client.ts.
The one generation policy: validates the domain request, applies model/tier policy, yields provider-neutral deltas; framework-neutral, reports nothing, shared by stream and job.
Single-role port in capability language: (request, { signal }) => AsyncIterable<ReplyDelta>. No SDK or HTTP vocabulary.
The single transport for the remote model provider: credentials, signal propagation, correlation ids, frame validation at the trust boundary, provider envelope to semantic code mapping.
Private adapter implementing the port over the transport; maps provider shapes to ReplyDelta and never leaks raw provider text.
Stream-channel machinery: awaits upstream acquisition before commit, pumps deltas as SSE events with ids, runs the sliding idle timer, emits in-band failures, and cleans up timers/listeners.
Server-only validated environment and provider credentials; fails at startup or first intentional access.
Browser async lifecycle: fetch + SSE parse, validates events, tracks last delivered id, resumes via Last-Event-ID, aborts on unmount.

flows: Stream happy path: browser POST /api/assistant/replies/stream -> route.ts decodes with a route-local schema, authenticates, builds identity {actor, tenant, requestId, traceId} -> creates one channel AbortController and links request.signal 'abort' to it -> stream.ts openReplyStream({identity, command, signal, deps}) -> server/open-reply-stream.ts AWAITS upstream acquisition -> application/generate-reply.ts -> ports/reply-generator -> server/reply-generator.ts -> server/provider-transport.ts (signal passed to the provider fetch) -> route returns Response with text/event-stream, no-store, X-Accel-Buffering: no (commit) -> each delta enqueued as `event: chunk` with an `id:` cursor -> `done` -> close.

Pre-commit failure: acquisition throws or returns a semantic failure before any Response exists -> route maps validation->400, unauthorized->401, forbidden->403, not_found->404, rate_limited->429 with Retry-After, unavailable->503, unknown->500 with a safe public body. Constructing a ReadableStream first and failing inside start() would not qualify as pre-commit, so acquisition is awaited outside it.

Post-commit failure: any failure after headers are sent emits an in-band {type:'error', code} event followed by close; the status is never changed. The adapter returns a clean semantic code with no raw provider message and no provider error attached as cause.

Sliding idle timeout: a timer is restarted on every upstream delta enqueue, so it bounds only the gap between tokens and never caps a long successful stream. Self-generated `:heartbeat` comments deliberately do NOT reset it. On fire, channel.abort(idleReason) makes the provider observe the abort, then an in-band {type:'error', code:'unavailable'} event is emitted and the stream closes.

Cancellation: request abort (client disconnect) and the response stream's cancel(reason) callback both call abort on the same channel-owned AbortController, whose signal was passed to the provider fetch, so the upstream producer actually observes it. A finally block clears the idle timer, removes the abort listener, and releases the reader. Disconnect is classified as cancellation, not a defect, and is not reported.

Report-once: the Route Handler is the sole capture owner and reports the unexpected failure once with request/trace context. stream.ts, application/generate-reply.ts, and the private adapters stay silent; the adapter records only approved diagnostic context internally.

Client resume: client/use-reply-stream.ts validates each event against client.ts, tracks the last delivered event id, and on a mid-stream transport drop reconnects with Last-Event-ID to resume rather than replaying the request.

Job: queue -> app/api/assistant/replies/jobs/route.ts verifies the signature and applies a durable idempotency key -> job.ts runReplyGeneration({identity, command, deadlineMs, attempt, deps}) -> the SAME application/generate-reply.ts with liveness = {kind:'deadline', deadlineMs} -> same port and transport. The job owns its own AbortController bound to its deadline, bounded exponential retry for unavailable/rate_limited, no retry for validation/forbidden/contract, idempotency so retries do not duplicate a reply, dead-letter after the attempt cap, and its own single failure report.

decisions.choice: One capability root src/modules/assistant-replies/ owning prompt policy, generation, stream events, and the job contract.
decisions.rationale: The stream endpoint, the provider, and the job serve one product goal under one policy and lifecycle. A transport, an endpoint, or a provider does not create a capability.

decisions.choice: A dedicated POST Route Handler that returns an SSE Response, not a Server Action.
decisions.rationale: A Server Action resolves to one serializable value and owns no headers or commit state. It cannot emit an in-band failure after commit, cannot expose a channel-owned AbortController that both the request abort and the response stream's cancel() drive into the provider fetch, and offers only a whole-request deadline rather than a per-token sliding timer. Browser-owned reads also do not belong on actions.

decisions.choice: Rejected for committed streams; resume via Last-Event-ID instead. Retry is kept where it is safe: pre-commit acquisition in the transport, and the job channel.
decisions.rationale: Once bytes are committed the client already holds tokens, so replaying the request duplicates them. Resume from the last delivered event id is the only correct recovery for a committed stream.

decisions.topic: One generic result wrapper for HTTP, stream, and job
decisions.choice: Rejected. Share semantic failure codes, reporter/request context, redaction, and provider-error mapping; keep channel-native outcomes separate.
decisions.rationale: HTTP owns status and headers, the stream owns pre- vs post-commit dispatch, and the job owns retry and dead-letter verdicts. A single returnable-failure carrier cannot express 'headers already sent, emit in-band and close', so the wrapper would silently break the required post-commit property.

decisions.topic: Shared application operation without shared liveness
decisions.choice: Both channels call application/generate-reply.ts, which takes liveness as a named policy input: the stream passes {kind:'idle', idleMs}, the job passes {kind:'deadline', deadlineMs}.
decisions.rationale: This preserves the stakeholder's reuse of one generation policy while preventing the job from inheriting stream idle-timeout semantics, which the skill forbids unless both channels intentionally share a named provider-liveness policy.

decisions.choice: Keep application/generate-reply.ts as a real operation rather than a forwarding call.
decisions.rationale: It survives the deletion test: it applies domain prompt invariants and model/tier policy and is genuinely shared by two runtime channels. Deleting it would push that policy into both the route and the job.

decisions.choice: One capability-shaped single-role port (request, {signal}) => AsyncIterable<ReplyDelta>, implemented by one private adapter over one transport module.
decisions.rationale: The core needs to name generation in application language independent of the SDK, with a real production consumer. The port is not mirrored on provider endpoints, and SDK and wire types stay in server/**.

decisions.choice: Await the upstream stream handshake before constructing or returning the Response.
decisions.rationale: It is the only way startup failures can still map to an HTTP status. Returning a Response first turns every provider auth, quota, or outage failure into a 200 followed by an in-band error.

decisions.choice: The Route Handler (stream) and the job callback route are the sole capture owners; stream.ts, the operation, and adapters stay silent.
decisions.rationale: One report per runtime operation, from the channel that can name the request and outcome. Reporting at both an adapter and the outer channel is an explicit failure mode.

decisions.choice: Only stream.ts, job.ts, and client.ts. No server.ts, rsc.ts, actions.ts, query-cache.ts, or ui.ts.
decisions.rationale: Each surface must have a named current consumer: the stream route, the job route, and app/** client components respectively. The task describes no RSC read, mutation, cross-capability composition, shared query key, or reused UI.

decisions.choice: Reuse the project's existing shared/kernel failure taxonomy if present; do not create a new shared root for this capability.
decisions.rationale: Shared admission requires at least two real capabilities with identical meaning and lifecycle. One capability cannot justify promotion.

decisions.choice: server-only in server/**, client-only in client/**, plus the path rules.
decisions.rationale: A production build must fail when a Client Component imports a server surface or provider credentials; path rules alone do not enforce that.

risks: The idle timeout is only correct if the timer resets on upstream progress. Resetting it on self-generated heartbeat comments would silently disable the property while appearing to work.
If acquisition is not genuinely awaited before Response construction, every startup failure degrades into a 200 plus an in-band error and the pre-commit HTTP mapping becomes dead code.
Buffering proxies and some edge runtimes can defeat commit semantics; no-store plus X-Accel-Buffering: no needs verification against the actual deployment target.
If framework instrumentation auto-captures rethrown exceptions, the route's report plus that capture double-reports the same defect. Pick one capture owner or carry an already-reported marker.
Resume correctness depends on the provider surfacing stable per-event ids. If it does not, publish that limitation rather than synthesizing a cursor that cannot be honored on reconnect.
Client disconnect must be classified as cancellation rather than an unavailable defect, or normal navigation away will pollute error telemetry and job-style alerting.

The shared operation is a real coupling point: if a future change to generate-reply.ts assumes stream framing or idle semantics, the job silently inherits them. The liveness policy input must stay the only channel-specific parameter.
Provider frame validation at the transport boundary is easy to skip because static SDK types look sufficient; unvalidated network payloads would let provider shapes reach the public event contract.
